sections.title: Named peoples and a present government
sections.text: The Tribe’s history identifies Wichita Proper, Waco, Taovaya, Tawakoni and Kichai within its account. Its later chapter describes the organized Wichita and Affiliated Tribes community at Anadarko. Keep those two levels clear: related historical peoples are not simply alternate spellings, and this institutional account does not make every historical group one timeless government. Other historical and community sources should be read with their dates and named scope. The dated Elam and Harper accounts also distinguish narrower and broader uses of Wichita; their historical terminology must be read in context.

sections.title: Farming, hunting and the seasonal village
sections.text: The People of the Grass House chapter describes a seasonal pattern combining gardens and buffalo hunting. It follows food preservation and storage alongside the work of maintaining grass houses. Read this as a historical account of particular Plains village practices, including cooperative household work, rather than a picture of how every Wichita person lives today. Cultural and ceremonial narratives in the original remain with their publisher.

sections.title: Red River trade and changing villages
sections.text: Harper places Taovaya settlements on both sides of the Red River and discusses related villages sharing trade centers. Her interpretation supports historical Texas connections while retaining separate names; it does not establish a fixed territory. The underlying colonial records remain unread here.

sections.title: Texas displacement and wartime refuge
sections.text: The Tribe’s Days of Darkness chapter recounts a Brazos River reservation in 1855, subsequent removal from Texas to the Washita River, and flight to Kansas during the Civil War. It describes hunger, disease, boarding-school pressure and later allotment as part of its history of dispossession. These are attributed elements of the institutional narrative. Underlying treaties, military files, registers and allotment records were not directly inspected in this community-source review.

sections.title: Continuity through family and community
sections.text: A New Beginning emphasizes continuing community after the loss of grass-house village life. The account describes older and younger generations sharing memories while people pursue education, employment and family gatherings. Its language of endurance is the institution’s interpretation of its history; it is not a statistical survey or a claim that every member has the same experience or practice.

sections.title: Community memory beyond a story of disappearance
sections.text: Bethke, Trabert and Gary McAdams’s collaborative research with Wichita and Affiliated Tribes brings community memories together with archives and low-impact archaeology. The authors describe how twentieth-century gathering places in Oklahoma helped sustain relationships through and after allotment. Their account connects older history with living Wichita people. It remains a specific community-based study: its published recollections and academic interpretation should be attributed, rather than treated as a survey of every community or a current legal boundary.

sections.title: A public route into the language
sections.text: The Tribe’s online dictionary pairs English vocabulary and phrases with Wichita forms and links many entries for pronunciation. Readers can follow this community-published resource directly. The listing was inspected, but recordings and apps were not tested. Resource availability alone does not establish current speaker totals, proficiency or learning outcomes.

sections.title: Education as a contemporary institution
sections.text: The Education Services Department describes support ranging from adult and vocational learning to undergraduate and graduate study. Its program account also discusses lending equipment for coursework. These are the publisher’s stated activities and aims. Funding, eligibility and application requirements vary; this guide does not promise assistance or report measured outcomes. The original pages remain the route to current details.

sections.title: Reading path and the scope of this foundation
sections.text: Begin with the Tribe’s connected history exhibit and its authorship credits, then follow its public language and education resources. Compare Harper’s selected trade-history pages with the collaborative twentieth-century study, keeping period names, memories and scholarly interpretation distinct. Original colonial manuscripts, treaties, removal records and the governing instrument still need direct review. This is a new cited source guide, not a comprehensive history or a community-reviewed account.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Five substantive works form a first community-centered foundation: one connected institutional history exhibit, an official public lexical resource, a detailed education-program account, a selected1953 trade-history study, and a collaborative2024 academic/community history. The four history chapters count once. Three supporting references and one unread municipal lead remain excluded. Direct primary records, the separate affiliated histories, governing text and wider nineteenth-century Texas coverage remain open. The collection has not yet reached adequate initial coverage, research completion or community review.
remainingLimits: Original treaties, Texas removal records, military files, mission/colonial sources, allotment documents and underlying archaeological evidence were not directly reviewed in this community-source task.

The different histories of Waco, Tawakoni, Taovaya, Kichai and Wichita Proper need specifically scoped research. The institutional included-peoples list does not establish all present descendants or governments.
The governing resolution was unreadable in the available retrievals; no provision, current consolidated law, jurisdiction or membership conclusion is drawn.
The dictionary listing was read, but audio/apps were not tested and current speaker numbers or learning outcomes were not established.

Direct inspection of French and Spanish originals or reliable critical editions remains open; no archival summary is counted as the document itself.
The relation among historical Wichita, Guichita, Taovaya, Waco, Tawakoni, Iscani and Kichai labels needs comparison across dates, languages and the communities' own accounts.
The Texas nineteenth-century history requires closer source review beyond this selected eighteenth-century trade discussion.
Archaeological affiliation does not by itself establish an exclusive people/site identity, present descent or a legal boundary.
